title: Olympics as a Stage
bigQuestion: How did the Olympic Games turn sport into a stage where nations show flags, argue and sometimes stay away?

story.title: A New Flag in Antwerp
story.kicker: In 1920 a white flag with five rings flew over a stadium for the first time.
paragraphs: It is August 1920 in Antwerp, Belgium. The First World War ended less than two years ago. Parts of Belgium are still in ruins. Yet the city has agreed to host the Olympic Games, and athletes from more than twenty nations have arrived.

A new flag goes up over the stadium. It is white, with five linked rings in blue, yellow, black, green and red. Pierre de Coubertin, the French leader of the International Olympic Committee, designed it in 1913. The war kept it from flying at a Games until now.

Some nations are missing. Germany, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey, the defeated side in the war, were not invited. The new Soviet Russia did not take part either. So the stage is open to many nations, but the host and the committee decide who gets a seat.

A Belgian fencer named Victor Boin steps forward. He speaks the first Olympic oath, a promise made on behalf of all the athletes. In a few weeks the crowds will leave. The flag will be handed to the next host city. The stadium is a stage borrowed for a short time.
story.think: Why might a country that just lived through a war want to host the Olympic Games?

lessons.title: Festival at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: The ancient Olympic Games were a religious festival for Zeus held at Olympia in Greece for more than a thousand years.
reading: Olympia is a valley in southern Greece. In ancient times it held a *sanctuary*, a holy place, for the god Zeus. Greek tradition dates the first recorded Games there to 776 BCE. Historians treat that date as a tradition, since later writers built the list of winners.

The Games were held every four years. The Greeks called that four-year gap an Olympiad and used it to count time. The oldest event was the stadion, a footrace one length of the stadium. Later festivals added wrestling, boxing, chariot races and the pentathlon.

Only free Greek men and boys could compete. Enslaved people and foreigners could not. Married women were generally not allowed to watch, according to the Greek writer Pausanias. Unmarried women at Olympia had their own footraces in honor of the goddess Hera, called the *Heraean Games*.

The festival lasted into Roman times. Historians usually place its end around 393 CE, under the Christian emperor Theodosius I, who banned pagan festivals. The exact final year is still debated. Earthquakes and floods later buried much of the site until excavations in the 1800s.

words.d: a holy place set apart for a god, where festivals and offerings were held
the four-year period between one Olympic festival and the next
footraces for unmarried women at Olympia, held in honor of the goddess Hera

look.title: Two Kinds of Visitor
look.text: Picture two people walking toward Olympia in the 400s BCE. One is a free Greek man from Athens who has trained for the stadion race. The other is a married woman from the same city. Both want to see the festival of Zeus.

check.why: The sanctuary at Olympia and its Games honored Zeus; the Heraean races honored Hera.

check.q: What was an Olympiad?
check.why: Greeks counted time in Olympiads, the four years from one festival to the next.

check.q: Why do historians call 776 BCE a traditional date?

The Romans invented it in 393 CE

check.why: The date comes from winner lists put together by later writers, so historians treat it as tradition.

lessons.title: Revivals Before 1896
lessons.mainIdea: Towns in England and Greece held 'Olympian' games decades before the modern Olympics began.
reading: Much Wenlock is a small market town in Shropshire, England. In 1850 a local doctor, William Penny Brookes, started the Wenlock Olympian Games there. They mixed footraces and cricket with prizes for reading and knitting. Brookes hoped exercise and learning would help working people in his town.

Greece held its own *revival* too. A rich merchant, Evangelos Zappas, paid for Olympic games in Athens in 1859. More were held in 1870 and 1875. Greece had won independence from the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s, and the games were meant to link the new nation to its ancient past.

In 1890 a young French educator, Pierre de Coubertin, visited Much Wenlock. Brookes held a special festival for him. Coubertin later built an international version of the idea. The modern Games came from these local attempts, not from nowhere.

This matters for how we read the history. Coubertin is often called the founder of the modern Olympics. That is true of the international committee he helped create. But a town doctor and a Greek merchant had already shown that the ancient name could draw crowds.

words.d: bringing back an old practice or event in a new form
local games started in 1850 in Much Wenlock, England, by Dr. William Penny Brookes

look.title: Three Founders?
look.text: Three people could claim a part in starting the modern Olympics. William Penny Brookes held Olympian games in an English town from 1850. Evangelos Zappas paid for Olympic games in Athens in 1859. Pierre de Coubertin visited Brookes in 1890 and later led an international committee.
look.prompt: Which person would you call the founder, and what fact from the reading supports your choice?

check.why: Dr. William Penny Brookes began the Wenlock Olympian Games in 1850.

check.q: Why did Greece hold Olympic games in 1859?
choices: To link the new nation to its ancient past

check.why: Coubertin visited Much Wenlock in 1890, and Brookes held a festival for him.

lessons.title: Athens, 1896
lessons.mainIdea: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896 with about 241 men from 14 nations.
reading: In April 1896 the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens. The main stage was the *Panathenaic Stadium*, an ancient stadium rebuilt in white marble. A Greek businessman, Georgios Averoff, paid for much of the rebuilding. Crowds filled its long, narrow seats.

The International Olympic Committee counts about 241 athletes from 14 nations. All of them were men. Many were students or members of private clubs, not national teams picked by trials. Some simply paid their own way to Greece.

The most famous result came in the *marathon*, a new long-distance race based on a Greek legend about a runner from the town of Marathon. A Greek water carrier named Spyridon Louis won it. For the host nation, his victory turned a sports meet into a national celebration.

The 1896 Games set patterns that lasted. A host city built or rebuilt a stadium. Athletes were sorted by nation in the results. And the Games were meant to move to a different city every four years, so no single country would own them.

words.d: an ancient stadium in Athens, rebuilt in marble, that hosted the 1896 Games
a long-distance footrace first held at the 1896 Games, named after a Greek legend

lessons.title: Rings and an Oath
lessons.mainIdea: The Olympic flag and the athletes' oath both first appeared at the 1920 Antwerp Games.
reading: Coubertin drew the five rings in 1913. He described them in the IOC's magazine, the Revue Olympique. The rings are blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white field. They are linked to show many parts joined together.

Coubertin wrote that the six colors, counting the white, could make the flag of every nation of his time. In later years many people said the rings stand for five continents. Either way, the flag is a *symbol*: an object that stands for an idea bigger than itself.

The flag first flew at the Antwerp Games in 1920. That year the Belgian fencer Victor Boin spoke the first Olympic *oath*. He promised, for all the athletes, to compete fairly and follow the rules. An oath for judges was added in 1972, and one for coaches much later.

Symbols like these gave the Games a ceremony that did not belong to any one country. Each host added its own music and flags. But the rings and the oath returned every time, linking one Games to the next.

words.d: an object or picture that stands for a bigger idea
a spoken, public promise
the IOC's magazine, where Coubertin described the rings in 1913

look.title: Coubertin on the Rings, 1913

look.cite: Pierre de Coubertin, article on the Olympic emblem and flag, Revue Olympique, August 1913
look.prompt: Coubertin linked the flag to colors, while later people linked it to continents. Why might an explanation of a symbol change over time?

check.q: When did the Olympic flag first fly at a Games?
check.why: Designed in 1913, the flag first flew at the Antwerp Games in 1920.

check.why: Belgian fencer Victor Boin spoke the first athletes' oath in 1920.

check.why: In 1913 Coubertin wrote that the colors together reproduced the colors of every national flag.

lessons.title: Marching as a Nation
lessons.mainIdea: Athletes enter the Games through National Olympic Committees and march behind their country's flag.
reading: At the first Games, some athletes entered on their own or through clubs. Over the next years the IOC required entries through a *National Olympic Committee*, or NOC. An NOC is a body in each country that picks and sends that country's team. The United States Olympic Committee grew from such a body.

The opening ceremony shows this system in public. Teams march into the stadium one country at a time, each behind its flag. Since the 1920s, Greece has usually entered first to honor the ancient Games. The host nation enters last.

The medal table in newspapers counts medals by country. The IOC does not officially rank nations, but the press has done so for over a century. That habit turns single athletes into a score for a whole nation.

The NOC system also means a place without an IOC-recognized committee cannot send a team. So questions about who counts as a nation, such as divided Germany after 1949 or Taiwan and China, became questions for the Olympic movement too.

words.d: the body in each country that the IOC recognizes to choose and send its Olympic team
the parade and program that begin each Games, with teams marching behind flags
a list, made mostly by the press, that counts Olympic medals by country

look.prompt: How does headline B change who the win belongs to? Use the idea of the NOC and the medal table.

choices: A body that picks and sends a country's team

check.q: In the opening parade, which nation traditionally enters last?

check.why: Greece usually leads the parade; the host nation enters last.

lessons.title: Berlin, 1936
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi Germany used the 1936 Berlin Games as a stage for its government, and many Americans argued about going.
reading: The IOC chose Berlin in 1931. Two years later, Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party took power in Germany. The new government pushed Jewish people out of German sports clubs. In the United States, many people called for a *boycott*: refusing to take part as a protest.

The Amateur Athletic Union, which controlled much American track, argued over the boycott. In December 1935 its members narrowly voted to send athletes. Avery Brundage, head of the American Olympic Committee, led the side that wanted to go.

German organizers added a new ritual. Under Carl Diem, a flame was lit at Olympia in Greece and carried by runners to Berlin in the first Olympic *torch relay*. Film director Leni Riefenstahl turned the Games into a film called Olympia. Both linked the Nazi state to ancient Greece.

Athletes' stories did not fit the government's message. Jesse Owens, a Black American from Ohio State University, won four gold medals. Helene Mayer, a German fencer with a Jewish father, was placed on the German team and won a silver medal. The stage was built for propaganda, but it held many stories at once.

words.d: refusing to take part in something as a protest
carrying a flame lit at Olympia to the host city, first done for Berlin in 1936
information spread by a government or group to shape what people believe

look.prompt: Which memory would you put first in a museum display about 1936, and why?

check.why: The first torch relay carried a flame from Olympia to Berlin in 1936.

check.q: What did the Amateur Athletic Union decide in December 1935?

check.why: The AAU narrowly voted to send athletes, rejecting a boycott.

check.q: How many gold medals did Jesse Owens win in 1936?
check.why: Owens won four gold medals at Berlin.

lessons.title: Melbourne and South Africa
lessons.mainIdea: Nations boycotted the 1956 Games over two wars, and the IOC shut out apartheid South Africa from 1964 to 1992.
reading: The 1956 Summer Games in Melbourne, Australia, faced two crises. In the autumn, Soviet troops crushed an uprising in Hungary. The Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland stayed home in protest. Egypt, Iraq and Lebanon stayed away over the *Suez Crisis*, when Britain, France and Israel invaded Egypt.

South Africa raised a different question. Its law of *apartheid*, or racial separation, kept Black South Africans off its national teams. Other nations and African sports leaders argued that such a team broke the Olympic rule against discrimination.

The IOC withdrew its invitation to South Africa for the 1964 Tokyo Games. In 1970 it expelled South Africa's Olympic committee. South Africa did not return until the 1992 Barcelona Games, after the country began to end apartheid.

These cases show two tools. A boycott is chosen by the nation that stays home. An *expulsion* is chosen by the IOC, which removes a member. Both use the Games as a stage to say something about a government.

words.d: South Africa's system of laws separating people by race, from 1948 into the early 1990s
removing a member from an organization
the 1956 invasion of Egypt by Britain, France and Israel over the Suez Canal

look.prompt: Who made the choice in each case? Which case is a boycott, and which is an expulsion?

check.why: These nations protested the invasion of Egypt during the Suez Crisis.

check.q: When did South Africa return to the Olympic Games?
check.why: After being shut out from 1964 and expelled in 1970, South Africa returned in 1992.

check.q: What is the difference between a boycott and an expulsion?
choices: A nation chooses a boycott; the IOC chooses an expulsion
check.why: A nation boycotts by staying home; the IOC expels by removing a member.

lessons.title: Montreal, Moscow, Los Angeles
lessons.mainIdea: Three Summer Games in a row, 1976 to 1984, were cut short by boycotts.
reading: In 1976 a New Zealand rugby team toured South Africa. African nations asked the IOC to bar New Zealand from the Montreal Games. The IOC said rugby was not an Olympic sport and refused. More than twenty nations, most of them African, left or stayed away.

In December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. President Jimmy Carter called for a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Games. In April 1980 the United States Olympic Committee voted to go along. More than sixty nations did not send teams, and American athletes who had trained for years stayed home.

In 1984 the Summer Games went to Los Angeles. The Soviet Union announced it would not attend, citing safety. Most of its allies in Eastern Europe joined it, though Romania came. Many historians read the 1984 boycott as a reply to 1980.
The chart shows how the number of nations rose and fell. Each boycott changed who stood on the medal stand. Record books from those years list real winners, but they did not face the full field.

words.d: the long rivalry, about 1947 to 1991, between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies
an action taken to pay back an earlier action

choices: A rugby tour of South Africa
check.why: The US-led boycott of Moscow protested the December 1979 invasion of Afghanistan.

check.q: Why did many African nations leave the 1976 Games?

check.why: They protested New Zealand's sporting contact with apartheid South Africa.

check.q: Which Eastern European nation went to Los Angeles in 1984 despite the Soviet boycott?

lessons.title: The Two Germanys
lessons.mainIdea: Divided Germany sent a joint team from 1956 to 1964, then two separate teams from 1968 until 1990.
reading: After the Second World War, Germany split in 1949 into West Germany and East Germany. Each had its own government and wanted its own Olympic team. The IOC recognized West Germany's committee first, in the early 1950s.

The IOC pressed the two states to share. From 1956 to 1964 they sent a *unified team*. It marched under one flag, black, red and gold with the Olympic rings, and used Beethoven's Ode to Joy in place of an anthem.

From 1968 the two Germanys competed as separate teams. East Germany built a state sport system that won many medals. Later it was revealed that the system gave many athletes performance drugs, often without telling them.

Germany reunited in October 1990. At the 1992 Games in Albertville and Barcelona, one German team competed again. The story shows that an Olympic team is a political decision about which government speaks for a people.

words.d: one Olympic team made from two or more states that agree to compete together
the joining of East and West Germany into one country in 1990

check.why: Germany reunited in 1990 and sent one team in 1992.

check.why: The joint team used Beethoven's Ode to Joy instead of either state's anthem.

lessons.title: Chicago's Lost Games
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago was chosen to host the 1904 Olympics, but the Games moved to St. Louis to join a world's fair.
reading: In 1901 the IOC chose Chicago to host the 1904 Summer Games. Chicago had hosted the World's Columbian Exposition in 1893, and its leaders wanted another world event. The University of Chicago's president, William Rainey Harper, was among the backers.

St. Louis was planning its own world's fair, the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, for 1904. Its organizers planned sports events of their own. The two cities competed for the same summer. The IOC moved the Games to St. Louis, where they became part of the fair.

The 1904 Games stretched over months and mixed with fair events. Few athletes crossed the ocean to reach the middle of America. The IOC counts only twelve nations, and most of the athletes were American. Historians often call these Games the weakest of the early modern era.
The story shows that a host city is a *bid*, not a birthright. Money, transport and other events decide where the Games land. Chicago bid again for the 2016 Games, and the IOC chose Rio de Janeiro.

words.d: a city's formal offer to host an event such as the Olympic Games
a large public exhibition where nations show inventions, goods and culture

lessons.title: Federations and the Program
lessons.mainIdea: International federations write one rule book for each Olympic sport, so athletes from many places can meet under the same rules.
reading: Before the modern Games, many sports had local rules. A footrace in America might be 100 yards, while one in France was measured in meters. To meet, nations had to agree on one set of rules and measures.

*International federations* do this work. Each one governs a sport across the world. Examples include FIFA for soccer, founded in 1904, the athletics federation now called World Athletics, founded in 1912, and FIBA for basketball, founded in 1932. The Olympics use metric distances set by these bodies.

The Olympic *program*, the list of sports, has changed often. Tug of war was an Olympic event from 1900 to 1920. Judo entered at the 1964 Tokyo Games, and taekwondo in 2000 at Sydney. Baseball was a medal sport from 1992 to 2008 and returned at the Tokyo Games held in 2021.

A sport joining the program usually adopts one world code. Local styles and rules may fade as athletes train for the Olympic version. So the Games can spread a sport widely while making it more alike everywhere.

words.d: a body that governs one sport across the world and writes its rules
the official list of sports and events at an Olympic Games
the measuring system based on meters, used for Olympic distances
